hero.title: Amending Act of 1781
hero.description: Also known as the Act of Settlement, this landmark legislation resolved the severe constitutional conflicts between the Supreme Court and the Governor-General-in-Council in Bengal.

cards.details: Established the Governor-General of Bengal and a Supreme Court at Calcutta, but left their respective jurisdictions vague, causing major administration clashes.
Passed to resolve the conflict between the judiciary (Supreme Court) and executive (Governor-General-in-Council). Exempted official acts and revenue matters.
Introduced the Board of Control to oversee political affairs, separating them from the commercial affairs managed by the Court of Directors.

mnemonics.title: Mnemonics & Memory Hacks
mnemonics.description: Use these visual memory hooks to retain critical facts about the Amending Act of 1781 for the UPSC Civil Services Examination.

items.title: Mnemonic 1: Official Exemption
items.decryption: Remember that the **Governor-General**, his **Council**, and EIC **Servants** were exempted from the Supreme Court's jurisdiction for their **OFF**icial acts.

items.title: Mnemonic 2: Revenue Separation
items.decryption: The Supreme Court was completely **Ex**cluded from having jurisdiction over **Rev**enue matters and collection acts.

items.title: Mnemonic 3: Judicial Hierarchy
items.decryption: Appeals from **Prov**incial Courts went directly to the **GG**-in-Council (functioning as Sadar Diwani Adalat), bypassing the Supreme Court.

flashcards.title: Active Recall Flashcards
flashcards.description: Use these active recall questions to reinforce fact-dense syllabus details on the Amending Act of 1781.

items.question: What is the alternative name for the Amending Act of 1781?
items.answer: The Act of Settlement 1781 or the Declaratory Act of 1781.

items.question: Which parliamentary committee recommended the Amending Act of 1781?
items.answer: The Touchet Committee, appointed to investigate the executive-judicial conflicts in Bengal.

items.question: How did the Act change the jurisdiction of the Supreme Court regarding EIC officials?
items.answer: It exempted the Governor-General, his Council, and Company servants from the Court's jurisdiction for acts done in their official capacity.

items.question: Were revenue matters under the Supreme Court's jurisdiction after 1781?
items.answer: No. The Act explicitly excluded revenue matters and acts done in the collection of revenue from the Supreme Court's jurisdiction.

items.question: Which body heard appeals from the Provincial Courts (Mofussil Courts) under this Act?
items.answer: The appeals lay to the Governor-General-in-Council, not the Supreme Court.

items.question: What did the Act specify regarding the personal laws of the defendants?
items.answer: The Supreme Court was required to administer Hindu personal law for Hindus and Mohammedan personal law for Muslims.

traps.title: UPSC Prelims Traps to Avoid
items: Trap 1: Do not confuse the Amending Act of 1781 with Pitt's India Act of 1784. The 1781 Act (Act of Settlement) dealt with executive-judicial separation, whereas the 1784 Act introduced the Board of Control and Double Government.
Trap 2: The Act did not abolish the Supreme Court of Calcutta. It only restricted its jurisdiction, exempting the Governor-General, EIC servants (official acts), and revenue matters.

Trap 3: The Act did not apply personal laws only to British subjects. It mandated that native defendants in Calcutta be tried under their respective personal laws (Hindu law for Hindus, Muslim law for Muslims).
Trap 4: The Governor-General-in-Council did not lose the power to make regulations. In fact, the Act of 1781 explicitly granted them the power to frame regulations for Provincial Courts and Councils.

sections.title: 1. Genesis of the Act: The Executive-Judicial Conflict (1773-1781)
sections.content:
The Regulating Act of 1773 had established a dual system of governance in Bengal: the Governor-General-in-Council (executive) and the Supreme Court of Judicature at Calcutta (judiciary). However, it failed to define the boundary between them, leading to severe clashes over authority, jurisdiction, and law.

Major Points of Friction
  • Jurisdiction over Zamindars: The Supreme Court claimed jurisdiction over all native inhabitants of Bengal, Bihar, and Orissa, including EIC revenue collectors (Diwans) and land-owning Zamindars. The executive argued this disrupted revenue collection.
  • Status of EIC Servants: The Court subjected EIC servants to its English common law rulings for their official administrative actions, causing administrative paralysis.
  • Personal Laws Ignored: English judges initially applied unfamiliar English common law principles to native cases, disregarding Hindu and Islamic customs.
Famous Conflict Cases

Patna Case (1777-1779): The Supreme Court penalized EIC revenue officers for executing judicial warrants, claiming supremacy over provincial administrations.
Cossijurah Case (1779-1780): The Governor-General Warren Hastings ordered Company troops to resist the execution of a Supreme Court writ against a local Zamindar, creating a physical standoff between the military and judicial bailiffs.

Executive-Judicial Clash Cycle (1773-1781)

sections.title: 2. Key Statutory Provisions & Constitutional Significance
sections.content:
The Amending Act of 1781 (Act of Settlement) brought crucial adjustments to the governing framework. It drew clear lines of authority, protected the administrative machinery from judicial interference, and recognized indigenous social realities.

Major Provisions of the Act
  • Executive Immunity: The Governor-General and his Council were exempted from the jurisdiction of the Supreme Court for acts done in their public capacity.
  • Revenue Separation: The Court had no jurisdiction over revenue collection, protecting the EIC's financial lifeline.
  • Personal Law Recognition: The Supreme Court had to respect religious and social customs of the defendants. Hindu laws applied to Hindu defendants, and Sharia laws to Muslim defendants.
  • Appellate Hierarchy: Appeals from Provincial Courts were routed to the Governor-General-in-Council, making the executive the supreme provincial court of appeal.
Constitutional Impact

The Act of Settlement of 1781 is historically significant as the first attempt to introduce a separation of powers in British India. By stripping the Supreme Court of its oversight on revenue administration and executive official duties, it ensured administrative stability at the cost of weakening the judiciary's check on executive power.

Legal & Executive Changes: Regulating Act (1773) vs. Amending Act (1781)

Feature Regulating Act of 1773 Amending Act of 1781
GG & Council Immunity Subject to Court's jurisdiction for official acts. Exempted from Court's jurisdiction for official acts.
Revenue Jurisdiction Supreme Court claimed jurisdiction over collections and officers. Completely excluded from Court's jurisdiction.
Applicable Law English Common Law (Vague guidelines). Personal Laws (Hindu law for Hindus, Sharia for Muslims).
Appeals from Provincial Courts Unclear path; Supreme Court claimed appellate rights. Routed to Governor-General-in-Council.
